questions.q: A complete Geographic Information System (GIS) requires several fundamental components to operate successfully. Which of the following is **NOT** classified as one of the basic components of GIS?
questions.explain: The five universally recognized components of a GIS are **Hardware**, **Software**, **Data**, **Procedures** (or methods), and **Experts** (people/personnel). While **satellites** are essential tools in remote sensing for *collecting* spatial data, they are not themselves considered a core component of the GIS environment.

questions.q: Which source of GIS data involves the process of tracing and converting existing printed topographical or thematic paper maps into a computer-readable digital format?
questions.explain: **Map digitizing** is the procedure used to transform physical, analogue maps into digital vectors or rasters (using a digitizing tablet or scanner) so they can be processed and analyzed by GIS software. By contrast, **remote sensing** involves capturing new images from aircraft or satellites.

questions.q: In the context of urban development in West African cities, how is a Geographic Information System (GIS) most practically utilized by town planners?
options: To physically construct drainage systems for new housing estates
To capture and synthesize atmospheric carbon emissions into tables
To model traffic flow patterns and enforce zoning of land use
To manually execute land surveys using a chain and prismatic compass
questions.explain: GIS is an analytical tool used to capture, store, analyze, and manage spatial data. Town planners use it to overlay different data layers (such as road networks, population density, and vegetation) to **model traffic flow, designate land use zones, and plan infrastructure**. It does not perform the physical engineering tasks (A) or manual land surveying (D).

questions.q: Despite its immense benefits in transportation routing and agricultural planning, the integration of GIS in many developing countries is severely limited by which of the following set of problems?
options: An oversupply of technical software and redundant experts
Inadequate capital funding and erratic power supply
The inability of computers to read coordinate geometry
Excessive reliance on traditional compass surveying methods
questions.explain: The syllabus highlights several key problems facing GIS adoption: **power, personnel, and capital**. In developing nations, the high cost of procuring advanced hardware/software (capital), the lack of highly trained geospatial analysts (personnel), and inconsistent electricity (power supply) are primary barriers to establishing effective GIS networks.
